transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-29
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 58 min
Attendees: Maya Chen, Raj Patel, Ana García (Redwood) / Lena Ortiz, Tomáš Novak, Priya Iyer, Ethan Clarke (HorizonMesh)

Summary (auto): Quick partner intro and scoping call. HorizonMesh is evaluating an onramp to provide managed LLM features inside their SaaS offering. Primary asks: predictable latency for real-time chat, cost controls, and a VPC/private deployment path for regulated customers. Redwood described Hosted/Dedicated/Private options and proposed a short benchmark and a design deep-dive.

00:00:05 Maya (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, um we're Maya chen from redwood inference, i'm the AE here, and with me is raj patel our solutions engineer, and ana who's supporting partner onboarding, um, excited to kick off.
00:00:18 Lena (HorizonMesh): thanks maya, yeah hi all, lena here. quick intro — horizonmesh builds embedded search and chat inside enterprise fleet management apps, so low latency for chat, and regulatory customers in eu/uk with data residency needs.
00:00:31 Tomáš (HorizonMesh): tomáš here, i'm the CTO. main things — we need to understand integration patterns and how redwood will fit into our multi-tenant infra. also curious about gpu reqs, and whether we should go hosted or bring dedicated nodes.
00:00:45 Raj (Redwood): cool, thanks. quick yes — i can walk through the options and then we can map to your constraints. just to set expectations: redwood offers hosted api for fastest time-to-value, dedicated reserved capacity for predictable throughput, and private/vpc packages for regulated workloads. each has tradeoffs on latency, cost, and operational management.
00:01:05 Priya (HorizonMesh): hey— i'm priya, solutions architect. want to call out that some of our customers need sub-200ms token latency for short prompts, and others are okay with higher latency but need strong audit logs + kms integration.
00:01:20 Ana (Redwood): noted — we have per-token latencies in our catalog and we also support KMS/HSM integrations for private. audit logs and SIEM hooks are part of our private deployment checklist.
00:01:33 Ethan (HorizonMesh): do you have examples of latency numbers on a10 vs a100? we mostly run on a mix today in our infra.
00:01:41 Raj (Redwood): yep, rough numbers — on a100 we'll usually see lower p50/p95 for long context, a10 is a great price/perf for many chat workloads. and t4 for cheap bulk embedding. i'll caveat that it depends on seq length and batch patterns — redwood runtime does continuous batching and prefix/KV caching so you get better per-token cost at scale.
00:02:03 Tomáš: when you say kv cache — is that kv store across requests or like kv-cache inside the model runtime? we've had some confusion in our team.
00:02:10 Raj: good q — it's KV cache inside the runtime (the key-value attention cache), plus optional prefix caching for common system prompts. not a separate redis by default, though we can connect to external caches. sometimes the transcribes says K-V cache or kevi cache — so docs have both, yeah.
00:02:29 Lena: got it. for compliance we need data not to leave eu region for certain customers; can private deployment fit that?
00:02:36 Maya: yes, private/VPC or on-prem can be regionalized — we ship a private control plane and the inference nodes run in-customer region. we also have managed options with redwood where control plane sits in our infra but data path stays in your vpc.
00:02:52 Priya: and SSO? we use SAML across our internal consoles.
00:02:56 Ana: we support SAML/SSO and role-based access controls; audit logs can be shipped to your SIEM.
00:03:03 Ethan: any customer references for edge-ish setups or on-prem?
00:03:07 Maya: a few fintechs and healthcare customers—i can share anonymized case studies.
00:03:11 Tomáš: ok let's shift to integration patterns — we're evaluating two routes: 1) call out to hosted redwood api per request (simplest) 2) dedicated reserved capacity (redwood-managed but isolated) 3) private on-prem / vpc where we bring nodes closer to data. what are the operational differences?
00:03:31 Raj: hosted is just api keys, simplest, pay-as-you-go — but less predictable latency under certain burst patterns. Dedicated gives you reserved gpu pools with SLA-backed throughput, guaranteed burst capacity and predictable unit economics. Private gives you full control, kms/hsm, audit highest level but you manage some infra or we provide an on-prem package. for each we provide same api surface so dev experience is consistent.
00:03:56 Lena: cost wise? we need to show our finance team a delta between hosted vs dedicated.
00:04:02 Raj: comon patterns — hosted best for low commit, quick launch. Dedicated becomes cheaper once you commit to steady QPS because reserved capacity lowers per-token cost. For rough math: if you have steady 10 RPS of 1k-token requests, dedicated often wins. We'll share a calc sheet — i'll put a sample spreadsheet.
00:04:21 Priya: what about quantization? some of our workloads could use int8 to drop cost. do you support quantized models?
00:04:27 Raj: yes — runtime supports quantized variants and we recommend quantization for non-LLM-critical contexts. we also provide model recommendations and quantization profiles via Redwood Optimize. note that for certain safety-critical outputs we prefer float16 stacks.
00:04:45 Tomáš: any caveat about multitenancy? we want to host multiple customers with different security postures.
00:04:50 Ana: dedicated is tenant-isolated at infra layer — separate pools per tenant if needed, and private deployments can map to your VPC segmentation. RBAC and per-route policies available in the console.
00:05:05 Lena: ok that's helpful. can we talk about pilot success criteria — what would you suggest?
00:05:10 Maya: typical pilot is 2–4 weeks: we do an initial integration with hosted or dedicated trial capacity, run a set of benchmark prompts (you provide your sample workload), measure latency, cost per 1k tokens, and quality regressions against a golden set. success criteria often: p95 latency under X ms, token cost under $Y, and no quality regressions. we'll propose specifics after we get your QPS distribution.
00:05:33 Priya: for latency thresholds, we need p95 under 300ms for our chat flow when sequence length < 256. is that realistic?
00:05:40 Raj: yes that's realistic on a10 for many models, with proper batching and KV cache. if you need p95 under 150ms you may need a100 or optimized model choices and tighter routing.
00:05:56 Tomáš: can redwood do routing by policy? say route low-latency traffic to premium pool and background to cheaper pool?
00:06:01 Raj: yes — smart routing exists; you can set policies by route, cost tier, region, or fallback model variants if capacity constrained.
00:06:12 Ethan: how does failover look? we need graceful degradation if dedicated pool gets saturated.
00:06:17 Ana: you can define fallback to hosted or a cheaper model variant automatically. the console exposes rollouts and canary traffic splitting.
00:06:26 Lena: from a partnership perspective, we're also thinking about co-selling and a bundled offering. what does Redwood expect from partners?
00:06:33 Maya: great q — typically we look for technical alignment, a joint go-to-market deck, and an initial reference pilot. legal — we have a partner agreement; we can start with a simple MOU.
00:06:44 Tomáš: ok. one more infra-specific — we already have Kubernetes clusters on GCP with GPUs from a couple suppliers. if we want private onramp, can redwood's runtime sit as containers inside our k8s?
00:06:56 Raj: yes — we provide an on-prem package that can run as k8s helm charts. it integrates with your KMS and VPC networking. note: depending on node types you might need custom kernel modules for certain accel tech. we'll surface the exact requirements in the infra spec.
00:07:14 Priya: do you handle model updates and rollouts? we need predictable behavior when switching model versions.
00:07:19 Ana: yes — we have rollouts with canary and A/B, plus automatic fallback policies. model pinning per route is supported.
00:07:27 Lena: any known limitations with LLM tool calling and function outputs? we use structured outputs a lot.
00:07:32 Raj: we support structured outputs and function/tool calling patterns. some older open models have quirks; we include model-specific heuristics. sometimes transcript will show 'function call' or 'functioncal' as a single word — docs clarify.
00:07:45 Tomáš: i want to flag network egress — if we're in eu and use hosted, will tokens cross outside region?
00:07:51 Maya: by default hosted may route to nearest region, but for strict egress you should use private or dedicated in-region. we can ensure data residency via regional dedicated clusters.
00:08:03 Ethan: what's the onboarding timeline? we have a Q1 go-to-market with a customer pilot starting mid-feb.
00:08:10 Maya: typical onboarding is 2–4 weeks to pilot for hosted, 4–8 weeks for dedicated depending on capacity reservation, and private can be 6–12 weeks with infra change windows. for a Q1 pilot starting mid-feb, we'd want to start initial scoping now and schedule a deep-dive in early november.
00:08:26 Priya: ok yes let's plan that.

-- Mid-call technical dive --

00:08:33 Raj: i want to dive briefly on batching — redwood uses continuous batching that aggregates requests across routes up to latency SLOs; this reduces per-token cost but we can tune batch windows per route. for real-time chat you typically set tight latency SLOs which reduce batch size.
00:08:52 Tomáš: is there a way to force single-request low-latency path?
00:08:56 Raj: you can configure a low-latency class with pre-warmed workers for premium traffic; that obviously increases cost but gives microsecond-level improvements.
00:09:06 Lena: are there observability hooks? we need token-level cost breakdowns for chargeback.
00:09:12 Ana: yes — console has per-route token cost, per-token latency histograms, traces, and the ability to export logs to bigquery/splunk.
00:09:23 Priya: security: is SOC 2/ISO in the standard pack?
00:09:27 Maya: redwood has SOC 2 and is pursuing ISO — i will share the latest compliance pack.
00:09:32 Tomáš: nice. any pitfalls with model quantization and hallucination? sometimes quantization increases weird outputs.
00:09:40 Raj: true — we run quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to evals and prompt sets; for high-criticality outputs we often stick with float16. we can also run shadow tests of quantized models before rollout.
00:09:55 Lena: perfect. let's talk pilot instrumentation — we'll supply a sample traffic trace and a golden set for quality. what's the minimal telemetry you need?
00:10:03 Raj: the basics — qps over time, sequence length histogram, common prompt types, and ideal p95 target. also any auth flow specifics if you're using SAML or service account mechanisms.
00:10:14 Tomáš: we'll get that to you by next tuesday.
00:10:18 Maya: great. i'll follow up with a short notes email and attach the private onramp doc and a benchmark template.

-- Closing and recap --

00:10:30 Maya: recap: redwood to share partner onboarding playbook + infra spec and benchmark sheet; raj to run initial benchmark; horizonmesh to send sample QPS/profile and legal/regulatory checklist. then schedule an infra deep-dive week of 2026-11-15.
00:10:45 Lena: sounds good, thanks everyone.
00:10:48 Priya: thanks, bye.
00:10:50 Tomáš: bye.
00:10:52 Raj: thanks all.
